html:
Virgil was the greatest poet of ancient Rome, author of the Aeneid, the epic of Rome's origins. He was born near Mantua in northern Italy in 70 BCE and died at Brindisi in 19 BCE.

His three works:

  • Eclogues, pastoral poems about shepherds, written around 39 BCE as the civil wars took farms from smallholders like his own family.
  • Georgics, a poem on farming, finished in 29 BCE, that praises work on the land.
  • Aeneid, written from 29 BCE until his death: twelve books on the Trojan prince Aeneas, who flees burning Troy, loves and leaves Queen Dido of Carthage, and fights his way to Italy to found the line that leads to Rome. It answers Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and honours Augustus as the heir of that destiny.

He belonged to the circle of Augustus's friend Maecenas and brought Horace, the poet of the Odes, into it. Dying with the Aeneid unrevised, he asked for it to be burned; Augustus refused. It became the school book of the Latin West for some 1,800 years. Christians read his fourth Eclogue as a prophecy of Christ, and Dante made him his guide through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy.
sum: Virgil was the greatest poet of ancient Rome, author of the Aeneid, the epic of Rome's origins. He was born near Mantua in northern Italy in 70 BCE and died at Brindisi in 19 BCE.
